name: Old English Period (Anglo-Saxon)
description: The literature of Anglo-Saxon England from the Germanic settlement of Britain to the aftermath of the Norman Conquest, composed in Old English (with a substantial parallel corpus in Anglo-Latin). The period runs from the earliest vernacular verse and the first written laws to the final prose of the early twelfth century, when the Old English literary language gave way to early Middle English.
historical_context: Bede dates the adventus Saxonum to c. 449; Germanic kingdoms (Kent, Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria, East Anglia) consolidated through the sixth and seventh centuries. The conversion of Kent under King Æthelberht and Augustine's mission of 597, the Synod of Whitby (664), and the monastic foundations of the seventh century created a literate Christian culture that absorbed the older Germanic poetic tradition. Viking raids beginning with Lindisfarne (793) led to the Danish settlement of eastern England and the wars of King Alfred (871–899); the West Saxon kings unified England in the tenth century; the Benedictine Reform of the 960s–980s revived monastic learning; renewed Scandinavian invasion ended with Cnut's accession (1016); and the Norman Conquest of 1066 ended the period's political independence, though Old English prose continued to be copied and composed for several decades afterward.
literary_characteristics: Old English verse is alliterative and accentual: a four-stress line divided by a caesura, linked by alliteration, built from formulaic diction, kennings, variation, and paratactic syntax. The surviving corpus (about 30,000 lines) is preserved in four principal poetic manuscripts — the Nowell Codex (Cotton Vitellius A.xv), the Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), the Vercelli Book (Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII), and the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11) — with heroic, elegiac, religious, and wisdom poetry often combining Christian and pre-Christian Germanic material. Prose develops from the late ninth century under Alfred's educational program into a sophisticated tradition of history, homily, hagiography, law, and translation, culminating in the rhythmical prose of Ælfric and Wulfstan. Anglo-Latin writing (Aldhelm, Bede, Alcuin) forms a parallel tradition of equal importance.
